title: Getting Started with Haven LLM Studio
excerpt: A complete walkthrough from installation to your first inference. Covers desktop, mobile, and SDK setup.
content:
Introduction

Welcome to Haven LLM Studio — your local AI inference powerhouse. This guide will walk you through everything you need to know to get Haven up and running, from initial installation to your first successful inference. Whether you're a developer looking to embed AI into your applications, a researcher experimenting with local models, or simply someone who values privacy and wants to run AI on their own hardware, this guide has you covered.

Haven LLM Studio represents a fundamentally different approach to AI inference. Rather than relying on cloud APIs that send your data to remote servers, Haven puts the entire inference stack on your machine. This means your prompts, responses, and usage patterns never leave your device. It also means you're not subject to rate limits, API costs, or service outages. Once set up, Haven works entirely offline, indefinitely.

Understanding the Architecture

Before we dive into installation, it's important to understand what Haven actually is and how its pieces fit together. Haven is built in layers, each serving a specific purpose:

The Native Core (C++) — At the bottom of the stack is a C++ wrapper around llama.cpp, the most widely-used open-source inference engine. This layer handles the actual computation: loading model weights from GGUF files, running matrix multiplications, managing the KV cache, and generating tokens. It's compiled specifically for your hardware, taking advantage of CPU instruction sets (AVX2, AVX512, NEON) and GPU acceleration (CUDA, ROCm, Metal, Vulkan).

The N-API Bridge — This is the glue between the native C++ code and Node.js. Using Node's N-API (Native API), Haven exposes the inference engine as a JavaScript module. This means you can call haven.infer() from JavaScript and it executes native C++ code under the hood, with zero HTTP overhead.

The API Server (Node.js) — Built on Express.js, this layer provides an OpenAI-compatible REST API. Any application that can talk to OpenAI's API can talk to Haven — just change the base URL. The server handles request routing, streaming responses via Server-Sent Events, model management, and real-time statistics broadcasting via WebSocket.

The Desktop UI (Electron + React) — A cross-platform desktop application that provides a visual interface for managing models, monitoring performance, and adjusting settings. Built with Electron for native system integration (system tray, file dialogs, notifications) and React for a responsive, modern UI.

The Mobile App (React Native) — A companion app for Android that serves two purposes: remote management of your Haven server (monitor stats, load/unload models, adjust settings from your phone) and on-device inference for sub-1B models running entirely on your phone's processor.

The SDK (@haven/sdk) — An npm package that lets developers embed Haven's inference engine directly into their Node.js applications without running a separate server process.

What You'll Need

Before we begin, make sure you have the following prerequisites installed on your system:

  • Node.js 20 or later — Haven uses modern JavaScript features and N-API version 9, which requires Node.js 20+. You can check your version with node -v. If you need to install or upgrade, visit nodejs.org or use a version manager like nvm.
  • CMake 3.20 or later — This is required to build the native C++ inference engine. CMake is a cross-platform build system that generates the appropriate build files for your operating system. Check your version with cmake --version.
  • Git — Needed to clone the repository and manage the llama.cpp submodule. Verify with git --version.
  • A C++ Compiler — The native layer is written in C++17 and needs to be compiled. On Linux, this means GCC 11+ or Clang 14+. On macOS, Xcode Command Line Tools (which include Clang). On Windows, Visual Studio 2019+ with the C++ workload.

Optionally, if you want GPU acceleration:

  • NVIDIA GPU — Install the CUDA Toolkit (11.8 or later). This enables Haven to offload model layers to your GPU for dramatically faster inference.
  • AMD GPU — Install ROCm drivers. Note that ROCm support is primarily available on Linux.
  • Apple Silicon — Metal is included with macOS. No additional installation needed.
  • Intel/AMD integrated GPU — Install the Vulkan SDK for cross-platform GPU acceleration.

Step 1: Clone the Repository

The first step is to get the Haven source code onto your machine. Open your terminal and run:

git clone https://github.com/Architect-Brad/Haven-LLM-Studio.git
cd Haven-LLM-Studio

This creates a new directory called Haven-LLM-Studio containing the entire project. The cd command moves you into that directory.

Step 2: Install Node.js Dependencies

Haven uses npm (Node Package Manager) to manage its JavaScript dependencies. Run:

npm install

This command reads the package.json file and downloads all required packages into a node_modules directory. This includes Express for the server, React for the UI, TypeScript for type safety, and various build tools. The initial install may take a minute or two depending on your internet connection.

Step 3: Initialize the llama.cpp Submodule

Haven depends on llama.cpp, which is included as a Git submodule. Submodules are a Git feature that lets one repository include another repository as a subdirectory. To download llama.cpp, run:

git submodule update --init --recursive --depth 1

The --init flag initializes the submodule, --recursive ensures any nested submodules are also initialized, and --depth 1 performs a shallow clone (downloading only the latest commit, which is much faster than the full history). This step downloads the llama.cpp source code into native/third_party/llama.cpp.

Step 4: Build the Native Layer

This is the most important step — compiling the C++ inference engine for your specific hardware. The build process varies depending on what hardware you want to use:

CPU Only (with AVX2 optimization)

./build.sh --avx2

This builds Haven with AVX2 instructions enabled, which are available on most x86 CPUs from 2013 onward (Intel Haswell and newer, AMD Zen and newer). If your CPU is older, you can still build without AVX2 by running ./build.sh --core.

NVIDIA GPU (CUDA)

./build.sh --cuda

This enables CUDA support, allowing Haven to offload model layers to your NVIDIA GPU. Make sure the CUDA Toolkit is installed and nvcc is in your PATH.

AMD GPU (ROCm)

./build.sh --rocm

This enables ROCm support for AMD GPUs. Note that ROCm is primarily supported on Linux.

Apple Silicon (Metal)

./build.sh --metal

This enables Metal support for Apple Silicon Macs. Metal is Apple's GPU acceleration framework and is included with macOS.

Android (Termux)

./build.sh --arm

This builds Haven with ARM NEON optimization for Android devices running Termux. NEON is ARM's SIMD instruction set, similar to AVX2 on x86.

Multi-GPU

./build.sh --cuda --multi-gpu

This enables multi-GPU tensor splitting, allowing you to distribute a model across multiple GPUs. You can combine any GPU flag with --multi-gpu.

The build process typically takes 5-15 minutes depending on your hardware. You'll see CMake configure the build, then compile the native code. If the build succeeds, you'll see a summary showing which features were enabled.

Step 5: Start the Server

Once the build is complete, you're ready to start Haven's API server:

npm run server

You should see a startup banner displaying your platform, CPU cores, memory, and inference mode. The server will be listening on http://127.0.0.1:1234 by default.

Step 6: Verify Everything Works

Open a new terminal tab and run a health check:

curl http://localhost:1234/health

You should receive a JSON response like:

{"status": "ok", "uptime": 5.2, "native": true}

The "native": true field confirms that the native C++ addon was loaded successfully. If it says false, the server is running in mock mode (placeholder responses) because the native addon couldn't be loaded.

Step 7: Load Your First Model

Before you can run inference, you need a model. Haven uses GGUF format models, which you can download from HuggingFace. Here's how to get started:

  1. Download a model — Visit HuggingFace and search for GGUF models. A good starting point is Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct-GGUF for testing, or bartowski/Meta-Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct-GGUF for a more capable model.
  2. Place it in your models directory — By default, Haven looks for models in ~/.haven/models/. Create this directory if it doesn't exist: mkdir -p ~/.haven/models
  3. Load the model — You can load a model via the API:
curl -X POST http://localhost:1234/api/models/load \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model_path": "~/.haven/models/your-model.gguf", "config": {"n_gpu_layers": 35}}'

Or via the desktop UI by clicking "Load" next to the model in the sidebar.

Step 8: Run Your First Inference

With a model loaded, you can now run inference:

curl http://localhost:1234/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello! What can you do?"}],
    "max_tokens": 100
  }'

You should receive a JSON response with the model's generated text. If you enabled streaming, the response will arrive token by token via Server-Sent Events.

Next Steps

Now that Haven is running and you've successfully run inference, here are some things to explore:

  • Try the desktop UI — Run npm run dev to launch the Electron desktop application with a visual interface for managing models and monitoring performance.
  • Explore the mobile app — If you're on Android, set up the React Native app to monitor your server remotely or run models directly on your phone.
  • Use the SDK — If you're building a Node.js application, install @haven/sdk and embed inference directly without a separate server process.
  • Set up cluster mode — If you have multiple machines, configure Haven's cluster mode for distributed inference.
  • Read the documentation — Check out the full documentation at /docs.html for detailed API references, configuration options, and troubleshooting guides.
💡 Pro Tip

Run ./first-run.sh instead of manual steps for an automated setup experience. This script checks all prerequisites, installs missing dependencies, builds the native layer with auto-detected hardware features, and starts the server — all in one command.

title: Understanding GPU Offloading in llama.cpp
excerpt: How layer offloading works, why it matters, and how Haven auto-detects the optimal configuration for your hardware.
content:
What is GPU Offloading?

GPU offloading is the technique of moving some or all of a neural network's layers from CPU memory (RAM) to GPU memory (VRAM). This is one of the most impactful optimizations you can make for local LLM inference, often resulting in 5-10x speed improvements.

To understand why this matters, we need to understand how transformer models work. A large language model like Llama 3.2 3B consists of 28 transformer layers stacked on top of each other. During inference, each layer performs matrix multiplications — essentially multiplying the input activations by the layer's weight matrices. These matrix multiplications are highly parallelizable operations, which is exactly what GPUs excel at.

A modern NVIDIA RTX 4060 can perform over 15 trillion floating-point operations per second (TFLOPS), while a typical CPU might manage 1-2 TFLOPS. For the matrix-heavy workloads of LLM inference, this difference translates directly into tokens-per-second.

How llama.cpp Handles Offloading

llama.cpp uses a parameter called n_gpu_layers (number of GPU layers) to determine how many of the model's layers should run on the GPU versus the CPU. This parameter accepts three types of values:

  • n_gpu_layers = 0 — CPU only. All layers run on the CPU. This is the default if no GPU backend is enabled.
  • n_gpu_layers = N (positive integer) — Offload exactly N layers to the GPU. The remaining layers run on the CPU.
  • n_gpu_layers = -1 — Offload all layers to the GPU. This is the fastest option if your GPU has enough VRAM.

The layers are offloaded in order, starting from the embedding layer and working through the transformer blocks. This means if you set n_gpu_layers = 10 on a 28-layer model, the first 10 layers (embedding + first 9 transformer blocks) run on the GPU, and the remaining 18 run on the CPU.

The Memory Equation

Understanding VRAM requirements is critical to effective offloading. Each layer of a model consumes a predictable amount of VRAM based on the model's size and quantization level. Here's a practical breakdown:

Model SizeQuantizationVRAM per LayerTotal VRAM (all layers)
0.5B (24 layers)Q4_K_M~15 MB~360 MB
3B (28 layers)Q4_K_M~130 MB~3.6 GB
7B (32 layers)Q4_K_M~230 MB~7.4 GB
13B (40 layers)Q4_K_M~380 MB~15.2 GB
70B (80 layers)Q4_K_M~800 MB~64 GB

These numbers include both the model weights and the KV cache (which stores attention information for the current context). The KV cache grows with context length — a 4096-token context uses roughly 2x the KV cache of a 512-token context.

A useful rule of thumb: you need approximately Model Size × 1.2 VRAM for full offloading. The 1.2x multiplier accounts for the KV cache and temporary buffers.

Haven's Auto-Detection System

One of Haven's key differentiators is its automatic hardware detection and optimization system. When Haven starts, it runs a comprehensive hardware analysis:

GPU Detection

Haven scans for available GPUs across multiple backends:

  • NVIDIA — Queries the NVIDIA driver via NVML (NVIDIA Management Library) to detect GPU model, VRAM, temperature, and utilization.
  • AMD — Reads from /sys/class/drm/ on Linux to detect AMD GPUs and their VRAM allocation.
  • Apple Silicon — Uses sysctlbyname to detect Apple Silicon and its unified memory architecture.
  • Intel/AMD iGPU — Detects integrated GPUs and calculates available shared memory (typically 40% of system RAM).

Memory Analysis

Haven calculates the total available memory across all detected GPUs and compares it against the model's requirements. It then recommends an optimal n_gpu_layers value:

  • If total VRAM ≥ model size × 1.2: recommends n_gpu_layers = -1 (full offload)
  • If total VRAM ≥ model size × 0.6: recommends partial offload proportional to available VRAM
  • If total VRAM < model size × 0.6: recommends minimal offload (5-10 layers) for the speedup on early layers

iGPU Special Handling

Integrated GPUs (Intel UHD, Iris Xe, AMD Radeon Graphics on APUs) share system RAM with the CPU. Haven detects this and applies special handling:

  • Reserves only 40% of available RAM for the iGPU (leaving 60% for the OS and other applications)
  • Recommends smaller batch sizes to avoid memory spikes
  • Reduces context size recommendations to prevent OOM crashes

Multi-GPU Offloading

When you have multiple GPUs, Haven uses tensor splitting to distribute layers across them. This is configured through two parameters:

{
  "multi_gpu": true,
  "tensor_split": [0.6, 0.4],
  "main_gpu": 0
}

The tensor_split array defines the proportion of model layers assigned to each GPU. These proportions should roughly match each GPU's available VRAM. For example, if you have an RTX 4070 (12GB) and an RTX 3060 (8GB), the split would be [0.6, 0.4] (12/20 = 60%, 8/20 = 40%).

The main_gpu parameter specifies which GPU handles the initial embedding and final output. This should typically be the GPU with the most VRAM.

Performance Expectations

Here's what you can realistically expect in terms of inference speed across different configurations, using a 3B model at Q4_K_M quantization:

ConfigurationTokens/secNotes
CPU only (AVX2)2-5Functional but slow. Good for testing.
CPU only (AVX512)4-8Significant improvement over AVX2.
Partial GPU offload (10 layers)10-20Noticeable speedup even with partial offload.
Full GPU offload (RTX 4060)30-60Excellent for interactive use.
Multi-GPU (2x RTX 4070)50-100+Near real-time for most use cases.

These numbers vary based on context length, batch size, and the specific model architecture. Longer contexts are slower due to the quadratic scaling of attention computation.

Practical Recommendations

Based on extensive testing, here are our recommendations for different scenarios:

For Interactive Chat

Set n_gpu_layers = -1 if your GPU has enough VRAM. If not, offload as many layers as possible. Even partial offload provides a noticeable speedup for the early layers, which handle the bulk of the computation.

For Batch Processing

Increase n_batch to 512 or 1024 if you have enough VRAM. Larger batch sizes process multiple prompts in parallel, improving throughput at the cost of higher memory usage.

For Memory-Constrained Systems

If you're running close to your VRAM limit, reduce n_ctx to 256 or 512. The KV cache scales linearly with context length, so halving the context roughly halves the cache size.

⚠️ iGPU Warning

Integrated GPUs share system RAM. Haven detects this and recommends conservative layer counts to avoid OOM crashes. If you experience crashes, reduce n_gpu_layers and n_ctx.

title: Building a Cluster: Multi-Node Inference
excerpt: Set up a Haven cluster across multiple machines. Master/worker architecture, load balancing, and monitoring.
content:
Why Cluster Mode?

Cluster mode is Haven's answer to a fundamental limitation of local AI inference: no single machine has infinite resources. Whether you're constrained by VRAM, compute power, or concurrent request handling, distributing the workload across multiple machines unlocks capabilities that a single node simply cannot achieve.

Here are the primary use cases for Haven's cluster mode:

  • Running models larger than any single machine's VRAM — By distributing model layers across multiple GPUs on different machines, you can run 70B+ models that would be impossible on a single consumer GPU.
  • Handling concurrent requests — A single Haven instance can only process one inference at a time. A cluster can handle multiple simultaneous requests by routing them to different workers.
  • Load balancing across heterogeneous hardware — If you have a mix of powerful and modest machines, the cluster automatically routes requests to the most capable available node.
  • High availability — If one worker goes offline, the cluster automatically reroutes requests to remaining nodes, ensuring continuous service.

Architecture Overview

Haven's cluster uses a master/worker architecture, which is a well-established pattern in distributed systems:

The Master Node acts as the coordinator. It receives all incoming inference requests, maintains a registry of available workers and their capabilities, selects the best worker for each request based on a scoring algorithm, and aggregates results. The master also monitors worker health through a heartbeat mechanism and removes unresponsive nodes from the routing pool.

Worker Nodes are the compute engines. Each worker runs its own Haven inference engine with its own model(s). Workers register with the master on startup, send periodic heartbeats with their current stats (VRAM usage, inference speed, active status), and execute inference tasks assigned by the master.

The communication between master and workers happens over WebSocket connections on a dedicated port (1235 by default, separate from the API server's port 1234). This ensures that cluster traffic doesn't interfere with API traffic.

Setting Up the Master Node

The master node is the brain of your cluster. It doesn't need to be the most powerful machine — its primary job is coordination, not computation. A modest machine with good network connectivity works well.

# Set environment variables
export HAVEN_CLUSTER=true
export HAVEN_CLUSTER_ROLE=master
export HAVEN_CLUSTER_PORT=1235
export HAVEN_MAX_WORKERS=10

# Start the server
npm run server

When the master starts, it initializes a WebSocket server on port 1235 and begins listening for worker connections. The HAVEN_MAX_WORKERS variable limits how many workers can join the cluster (default: 10).

Setting Up Worker Nodes

Each worker node needs to know where to find the master. On each worker machine, set the following environment variables:

export HAVEN_CLUSTER=true
export HAVEN_CLUSTER_ROLE=worker
export HAVEN_MASTER_URL=ws://192.168.1.100:1235
export HAVEN_NODE_ID=worker-1
export HAVEN_NODE_NAME="GPU Node 1"

# Start the server
npm run server

The HAVEN_MASTER_URL should point to your master node's IP address and cluster port. The HAVEN_NODE_ID should be unique across all workers — this is how the master identifies each worker. The HAVEN_NODE_NAME is a human-readable label that appears in monitoring dashboards.

The Load Balancing Algorithm

When the master receives an inference request, it needs to decide which worker should handle it. Haven uses a weighted scoring algorithm that considers two factors:

score = (available_vram / total_vram) × 0.7 + (1 - is_busy) × 0.3

The first component (70% weight) measures available VRAM as a proportion of total VRAM. Workers with more free VRAM score higher, ensuring that large models are routed to nodes that can accommodate them. The second component (30% weight) measures current load — workers that are currently processing a request score lower, preventing request queuing.

This weighting was chosen through extensive testing. VRAM is the primary bottleneck for LLM inference (you can't run a model that doesn't fit in memory), so it gets the higher weight. Current load is secondary but still important for maintaining low latency.

Heartbeat and Health Checks

The master maintains awareness of each worker's status through a heartbeat mechanism:

  • Heartbeat interval: Workers send their current stats (CPU usage, memory usage, VRAM usage, inference speed, active status) every 5 seconds via WebSocket.
  • Heartbeat timeout: If the master doesn't receive a heartbeat from a worker within 15 seconds (3 missed heartbeats), it marks the worker as offline and removes it from the routing pool.
  • Auto-reconnect: If a worker loses its connection to the master (network hiccup, master restart), it automatically attempts to reconnect every 5 seconds.
  • Graceful degradation: When a worker goes offline, any in-flight requests to that worker are marked as failed. The master logs the failure and routes subsequent requests to remaining workers.

Monitoring Your Cluster

Haven provides several ways to monitor your cluster's health and performance:

API Endpoints

# Check overall cluster status
curl http://localhost:1234/api/cluster/status

# List all nodes with their details
curl http://localhost:1234/api/cluster/nodes

# Route inference through the cluster
curl -X POST http://localhost:1234/api/cluster/infer \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"prompt": "Hello", "config": {}}'

WebSocket Stats

Connect to ws://localhost:1234/ws for real-time stats streaming. The master broadcasts cluster-wide stats every second, including total available VRAM across all workers, average inference speed, and active request count.

Desktop UI

If you're running the Haven desktop application, the cluster view shows all connected workers with their status, VRAM usage, and current load. Workers are color-coded: green for online, yellow for degraded, red for offline.

📘 Best Practice

Use machines with similar GPU capabilities for best load balancing results. Mixing an RTX 4090 with an integrated GPU will cause uneven distribution, as the 4090 will handle most requests while the iGPU sits idle. If you must mix hardware, consider running different models on different nodes rather than using cluster mode.

title: Running LLMs on Your Phone
excerpt: Sub-1B models on Android. Thermal management, battery optimization, and the best models for mobile inference.
content:
Yes, Your Phone Can Run LLMs

It sounds counterintuitive — running artificial intelligence models on a device designed for social media and photography. But modern smartphones are surprisingly capable inference machines. The key insight is that while phones don't have dedicated GPUs, their ARM processors include NEON SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) instructions that can process multiple data points in parallel, similar to how GPUs accelerate matrix operations.

Sub-1B models (models with fewer than 1 billion parameters) are small enough to fit entirely in a phone's RAM and fast enough to generate text at a usable speed. With proper optimization, you can achieve 4-12 tokens per second on modern Android devices — enough for a responsive chat experience.

Supported Models

Not all models are created equal when it comes to mobile inference. Here are the models we've tested and recommend for on-device use:

ModelParametersSize (Q4_K_M)RAM NeededExpected Speed
SmolLM-360M360M~220 MB~800 MB8-12 t/s
Qwen2.5-0.5B0.5B~350 MB~1 GB6-10 t/s
TinyLlama-1.1B1.1B~670 MB~1.5 GB4-7 t/s
Phi-3-mini-3.8B3.8B~2.2 GB~4 GB2-4 t/s

The "RAM Needed" column includes the model weights plus the KV cache for a 512-token context. If you increase the context size, you'll need proportionally more RAM.

How It Works Under the Hood

Haven's mobile app includes a native C++ inference engine compiled specifically for Android ARM64. Here's the technical breakdown:

NEON SIMD Optimization — ARM's NEON instruction set allows processing 4 or 8 floating-point values in a single instruction. Haven's native layer uses NEON-optimized matrix multiplication kernels from llama.cpp, which provide a 3-4x speedup over non-vectorized CPU inference.

Foreground Service — Android aggressively kills background processes that consume CPU or battery. Haven prevents this by running as a foreground service with a persistent notification. This tells Android's process manager that Haven is actively being used and should not be killed.

Wake Lock — Android's Doze mode puts the CPU to sleep when the screen is off to save battery. Haven acquires a partial wake lock during inference, which keeps the CPU awake without preventing the device from sleeping entirely. This is released immediately after inference completes.

Thermal Management

Phones throttle their CPUs when they get hot to prevent damage. Haven monitors your device's thermal status through Android's ThermalManager API and adjusts inference parameters accordingly:

  • Normal — Full speed. No throttling applied.
  • Light — Slight reduction in batch size. You probably won't notice the difference.
  • Moderate — Reduced batch size and context length. Inference will be noticeably slower.
  • Severe — Significant throttling. Haven displays a warning and suggests taking a break.
  • Critical — Inference is paused until the device cools down. Continuing could damage the device.

This thermal management is crucial for sustained use. Without it, your phone could overheat during long conversations, leading to aggressive throttling or even shutdown.

Battery Optimization

Android's battery optimization features are designed to extend battery life by restricting background apps. Unfortunately, this conflicts with Haven's need to run inference in the background. Haven addresses this in three ways:

  1. Foreground Service — As mentioned, the foreground service with persistent notification exempts Haven from most background restrictions.
  2. Battery Optimization Exemption — Haven can request that Android exclude it from battery optimization. This is done through Settings → Battery Optimization, or programmatically via the REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS permission.
  3. Efficient Inference — Haven's NEON-optimized engine is designed to complete inference as quickly as possible, minimizing the time the CPU runs at high frequency.

Performance Expectations by Device

Different phones have different capabilities. Here's what you can expect on popular devices, using SmolLM-360M at Q4_K_M:

DeviceChipsetSpeed (t/s)Notes
Pixel 8Tensor G38-12Excellent NEON performance.
Samsung S24Snapdragon 8 Gen 310-15Best-in-class mobile inference.
Galaxy A16Dimensity 63004-7Good for casual use.
Mid-range (Snapdragon 7 series)Various4-7Functional for short responses.
Budget (Unisoc, older MediaTek)Various2-4Slow but usable for simple tasks.

These speeds are for the first token (prefill). Subsequent tokens may be slightly faster as the KV cache is already populated.

Downloading Models on Your Phone

Haven's mobile app includes a built-in Model Browser that connects to HuggingFace's API. You can search for GGUF models, browse available quantizations, and download directly to your phone. Downloads are resumable, so if your connection drops, you can pick up where you left off.

Downloaded models are stored in ~/.haven/models/ on your device's internal storage. You can also manually copy GGUF files to this directory using a file manager or ADB.

✅ Fully Offline

Once the model is downloaded, all inference happens on-device. No internet connection required. Your conversations never leave your phone.

title: KDE Integration: A Native Experience
excerpt: System tray, D-Bus, KRunner, and Plasma widgets. Making Haven feel at home on Linux desktops.
content:
Haven on Linux Desktop

Linux users deserve more than an Electron app that happens to run on their desktop. Haven's KDE integration makes it feel like a native Plasma application, with system tray integration, D-Bus service discovery, KRunner search, and a desktop widget. This isn't just about aesthetics — it's about making Haven accessible through the workflows Linux users already know and love.

System Tray Integration

When Haven starts on a Linux desktop with a system tray (KDE Plasma, GNOME with extensions, XFCE, etc.), it adds an icon to the tray area. Right-clicking the icon reveals a context menu with quick actions:

  • Open Haven LLM Studio — Brings the main window to the foreground.
  • Start Server — Starts the Haven API server if it's not already running.
  • Stop Server — Gracefully stops the server, unloading any loaded models.
  • Load Model — Opens a file dialog to select and load a GGUF model.
  • Settings — Opens the settings dialog.
  • Quit — Exits Haven completely.

The tray icon also provides visual status feedback: a green icon means the server is running, yellow means it's starting up, and red means it's stopped or encountered an error.

D-Bus Service

D-Bus is the standard inter-process communication system on Linux desktops. Haven registers a D-Bus service at com.havenllm.Studio, which means any application on your system can control Haven programmatically.

The service exposes the following methods:

StartServer(port) → bool
StopServer() → bool
IsRunning() → bool
Infer(prompt, config) → string
GetStats() → string
LoadModel(path) → bool
UnloadModel() → bool
ListModels() → string

You can interact with the service from the command line using qdbus or busctl:

# Check if Haven is running
qdbus com.havenllm.Studio /com/havenllm/Studio com.havenllm.Studio.IsRunning

# Start the server on port 1234
qdbus com.havenllm.Studio /com/havenllm/Studio com.havenllm.Studio.StartServer 1234

# Run inference
qdbus com.havenllm.Studio /com/havenllm/Studio com.havenllm.Studio.Infer "Hello" "{}"

This D-Bus integration enables powerful automation scenarios. You could create a KDE Connect plugin to control Haven from your phone, a Konsole shortcut to run quick queries, or a custom Plasma widget that displays inference stats.

KRunner Plugin

KRunner is KDE's universal search and command launcher (activated by pressing Alt+F2). Haven installs a KRunner plugin that lets you query your local LLM directly from the search bar:

Alt+F2 → "ask haven What is quantum computing?"

The plugin sends your query to Haven's API and displays the response in a notification. This is perfect for quick questions without opening a browser or terminal.

The plugin is written in Python 3 and uses the dbus-next library to communicate with Haven's D-Bus service. To install the dependency:

pip install dbus-next

Plasma Widget

Haven includes a Plasma 6 widget that you can add to your desktop or panel. The widget displays:

  • Server status indicator (online/offline with color coding)
  • Current loaded model name
  • Real-time tokens/sec display
  • CPU usage percentage
  • A quick inference input field

To add the widget, right-click your desktop or panel, select "Add Widgets," search for "Haven LLM Studio," and drag it to your desired location.

Installation

All KDE integration components are installed with a single command:

./integrations/kde/install.sh

This script installs the desktop entry (for the application menu), D-Bus service definition, KRunner plugin, and Plasma widget. After installation, you may need to restart KRunner (kquitapp krunner && krunner) and Plasma (plasmashell --replace &) for all components to be recognized.

📘 Note

KRunner requires Python 3 with dbus-next. Install with pip install dbus-next. The Plasma widget requires Plasma 6. For Plasma 5, a separate widget is planned.

title: AVX2 vs AVX512 vs NEON: CPU Benchmarks
excerpt: Comprehensive performance comparison of CPU backends across different hardware platforms.
content:
CPU Inference Performance

Not everyone has a GPU, and that's perfectly fine. Haven optimizes CPU inference with three instruction sets: AVX2, AVX512, and ARM NEON. Understanding the performance differences between these backends helps you make informed decisions about hardware purchases and configuration.

Test Setup

All benchmarks were conducted under controlled conditions to ensure fair comparison:

  • Model: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (Q4_K_M quantization)
  • Prompt: 50 tokens (standard system prompt + user query)
  • Generation: 128 tokens
  • Settings: temperature=0.8, top_k=40, top_p=0.9, n_ctx=512
  • Environment: Each system was idle except for the inference process. No background tasks were running.

Results

HardwareBackendTokens/secRelative Performance
Intel i9-14900K (24 cores)AVX51212.4100%
Intel i9-14900K (24 cores)AVX29.879%
AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (16 cores)AVX51211.290%
AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (16 cores)AVX28.972%
Apple M3 Max (16 cores)NEON18.6150%
Raspberry Pi 5 (4 cores)NEON2.117%
Intel i5-12400 (6 cores)AVX25.242%
AMD Ryzen 5 5600X (6 cores)AVX24.839%

Key Findings

1. AVX512 is 25-30% Faster Than AVX2

The wider vector registers (512-bit vs 256-bit) make a significant difference for matrix operations. AVX512 can process twice as many floating-point values per instruction compared to AVX2. However, the actual speedup is only 25-30% because not all operations in the inference pipeline are vectorizable — some operations (like token sampling and KV cache management) are inherently sequential.

2. Apple Silicon Dominates

The M3 Max's NEON implementation outperforms even high-end x86 CPUs by a significant margin. This is due to several factors: the unified memory architecture (eliminating the CPU-GPU memory transfer bottleneck), the high memory bandwidth (400 GB/s on the M3 Max), and Apple's custom NEON implementation optimized for matrix operations.

3. Raspberry Pi is Viable

At 2.1 tokens per second, the Raspberry Pi 5 is slow but functional for small models and short responses. This makes it suitable for edge deployments, IoT applications, or educational purposes where cost is more important than speed.

4. Core Count Matters Less Than You'd Think

Notice that the 24-core i9-14900K is only ~40% faster than the 6-core i5-12400. This is because llama.cpp's threading model has diminishing returns beyond 8-12 cores. The bottleneck shifts from compute to memory bandwidth as you add more cores.

Recommendations

For Desktop Users

If your CPU supports AVX512 (AMD Zen 4+, Intel Sapphire Rapids+), always use it. The 25-30% speedup is significant for interactive use. If your CPU only supports AVX2 (most CPUs from 2013-2023), it's still perfectly usable — just expect slower speeds.

For Laptop Users

Apple Silicon laptops offer the best CPU inference performance in a portable form factor. The M3 Max achieves 18.6 t/s without a discrete GPU, which is faster than many desktop CPUs with dedicated GPUs.

For ARM Devices

NEON is mandatory on ARM — there's no fallback. All modern ARM processors (Apple Silicon, Snapdragon, Dimensity, Raspberry Pi) support NEON. Performance scales with core count and memory bandwidth.

⚠️ CPU vs GPU

Even the fastest CPU (18.6 t/s on M3 Max) is slower than a mid-range GPU (40-60 t/s on RTX 4060). Use CPU inference when GPU is unavailable, not as a replacement. The ideal setup is CPU + GPU, with the GPU handling the bulk of the computation.

title: Understanding Model Quantization: Q4 vs Q5 vs Q8
excerpt: A comprehensive guide to GGUF quantization methods, their impact on quality, and how to choose the right one for your hardware.
content:
What is Quantization?

Quantization is the process of reducing the precision of a model's weights from their original format (typically 16-bit floating point, or FP16) to a lower-precision format (like 4-bit or 8-bit integers). This is one of the most important optimizations for local LLM inference because it directly affects three critical factors: model size, memory requirements, and inference speed.

Think of it like compressing a high-resolution image. A 4K photo looks amazing but takes up a lot of storage. If you compress it to 1080p, it's much smaller and faster to load, and most people can't tell the difference on a phone screen. Quantization does the same thing for neural network weights — it reduces precision in ways that minimally impact the model's output quality.

How Quantization Works

Neural network weights are typically stored as 16-bit floating point numbers (FP16), which can represent values from approximately 0.00006 to 65,504 with about 3-4 decimal digits of precision. Quantization maps these FP16 values to a smaller set of discrete values — for example, 4-bit integers can only represent 16 distinct values (0-15).

The challenge is doing this mapping intelligently. A naive approach (simply rounding each weight to the nearest 4-bit value) would destroy the model's quality. Modern quantization methods use sophisticated techniques:

  • Group-wise quantization — Instead of quantizing the entire weight matrix with a single scale factor, the matrix is divided into small groups (typically 32 weights), and each group gets its own scale factor. This preserves more information because different parts of the matrix may have different value ranges.
  • Importance-aware quantization — Some weights are more important than others. K-quants (the "K" in Q4_K_M) identify and preserve the most important weights at higher precision while aggressively quantizing less important ones.
  • Outlier handling — Some weights are extreme outliers (much larger or smaller than the rest). Special handling for these outliers prevents them from distorting the quantization scale for the rest of the group.

GGUF Quantization Types

GGUF (GGML Universal Format) supports a wide range of quantization methods. Here's a comprehensive comparison:

TypeBits/WeightSize (7B)Quality LossBest For
Q2_K2.562.7 GBSignificantMaximum speed, minimal RAM
Q3_K_S3.253.1 GBModerateTight memory constraints
Q3_K_M3.663.5 GBModerateBalance of size and quality
Q4_K_M4.594.1 GBMinimalRecommended for most users
Q5_K_M5.534.7 GBNegligibleHigher quality when VRAM allows
Q6_K6.595.4 GBNear-zeroNear-FP16 quality
Q8_08.56.7 GBNoneFP16 equivalent
FP161613 GBNoneReference quality

The K-Quants Revolution

Modern GGUF quantization uses "K-quants," which represent a significant advancement over earlier methods. The key innovation is that K-quants apply different bit-widths to different weight groups within the same model. Important weights (like those in attention layers) get higher precision, while less critical weights (like those in feed-forward layers) get compressed more aggressively.

This is why Q4_K_M can retain ~95% of FP16 quality despite using only 4.59 bits per weight on average — it's not uniformly 4-bit. Some weights are effectively 5-bit or 6-bit, while others are 3-bit or 4-bit.

How to Choose the Right Quantization

The choice depends on your priorities:

Choose Q4_K_M if:

  • You want the best balance of quality and file size
  • You have moderate VRAM (4-8 GB for a 7B model)
  • You're running interactive chat or general-purpose tasks
  • This is your first time running a local model

Choose Q5_K_M if:

  • You have enough VRAM and want higher quality
  • You're doing creative writing or complex reasoning
  • You notice quality issues with Q4_K_M

Choose Q3_K_M if:

  • You're tight on memory
  • You're running a large model (13B+) on limited hardware
  • Speed is more important than quality

Choose Q8_0 if:

  • Quality is paramount and memory isn't an issue
  • You're benchmarking or evaluating model capabilities
  • You have a high-end GPU with plenty of VRAM

Quality Impact in Practice

Studies and community benchmarks consistently show that Q4_K_M retains approximately 95% of FP16 quality on standard benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC). The difference is often imperceptible in casual use — most users cannot distinguish between Q4_K_M and FP16 outputs in a blind test.

The quality loss becomes more noticeable with lower quantizations (Q2_K, Q3_K_S), particularly for complex reasoning tasks, code generation, and nuanced language understanding. For simple tasks like summarization, translation, or casual conversation, even Q3_K_M performs adequately.

📘 Pro Tip

Always test a model at Q4_K_M first. If quality is insufficient, try Q5_K_M. If it's too slow or doesn't fit in memory, try Q3_K_M. This iterative approach ensures you find the sweet spot for your specific use case and hardware.

title: Using Embedding Models with Haven
excerpt: Learn how to generate and use text embeddings for semantic search, RAG, and clustering with Haven's native embedding support.
content:
What are Embeddings?

Embeddings are dense vector representations of text. Instead of representing a sentence as a sequence of words, an embedding represents it as a list of numbers (typically 384 to 4096 numbers). The magic of embeddings is that semantically similar texts produce similar vectors. "The quick brown fox" and "A fast brown fox" will have very similar embedding vectors, while "The quick brown fox" and "Quantum physics is fascinating" will have very different vectors.

This property enables a wide range of applications:

  • Semantic Search — Find documents that are conceptually similar to a query, even if they don't share exact keywords.
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) — Retrieve relevant context from a knowledge base and inject it into the prompt for more accurate responses.
  • Clustering — Group similar documents together for organization and analysis.
  • Classification — Categorize text by comparing its embedding to known category embeddings.
  • Deduplication — Find near-duplicate documents by comparing embedding similarity.

Supported Embedding Models

Haven supports any GGUF embedding model. Here are the most popular options:

ModelParametersDimensionsSize (Q4)Best For
nomic-embed-text137M768274 MBGeneral-purpose semantic search
mxbai-embed-large335M1024670 MBHigh-accuracy retrieval
all-MiniLM-L6-v222M38480 MBFast, lightweight embedding
bge-large-en335M1024670 MBBenchmark-leading accuracy

Generating Embeddings

Using Haven's embedding API is straightforward:

curl -X POST http://localhost:1234/v1/embeddings \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "input": "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog",
    "model": "nomic-embed-text"
  }'

The response contains a normalized embedding vector:

{
  "object": "list",
  "data": [{
    "object": "embedding",
    "index": 0,
    "embedding": [0.023, -0.045, 0.012, ...]  // 768 values
  }],
  "model": "nomic-embed-text",
  "usage": { "prompt_tokens": 10, "total_tokens": 10 }
}

The embedding is L2-normalized (the vector has a length of 1), which simplifies similarity calculations. For normalized vectors, cosine similarity is equivalent to the dot product.

Using Embeddings for Semantic Search

Here's a complete example of building a semantic search system:

import { Haven } from '@haven/sdk';

const haven = new Haven();
await haven.loadModel('~/.haven/models/nomic-embed-text.Q4_K_M.gguf');

// Your document collection
const documents = [
  'How to install Node.js on Ubuntu',
  'Understanding GPU offloading in llama.cpp',
  'Building a REST API with Express',
  'Deploying applications with Docker',
  'Introduction to machine learning',
];

// Embed all documents
const docEmbeddings = await Promise.all(
  documents.map(doc => haven.embed(doc))
);

// Search function
async function search(query, topK = 3) {
  const queryEmbed = await haven.embed(query);
  
  const results = documents.map((doc, i) => ({
    text: doc,
    similarity: cosineSimilarity(queryEmbed.embedding, docEmbeddings[i].embedding),
  }));
  
  return results
    .sort((a, b) => b.similarity - a.similarity)
    .slice(0, topK);
}

function cosineSimilarity(a, b) {
  const dot = a.reduce((sum, v, i) => sum + v * b[i], 0);
  const normA = Math.sqrt(a.reduce((sum, v) => sum + v * v, 0));
  const normB = Math.sqrt(b.reduce((sum, v) => sum + v * v, 0));
  return dot / (normA * normB);
}

// Search
const results = await search('How do I set up Node.js on Linux?');
console.log(results);

Building a RAG Pipeline

Retrieval-Augmented Generation combines embedding-based retrieval with LLM generation to produce more accurate, context-aware responses:

  1. Embed the user query — Convert the question into an embedding vector.
  2. Find relevant chunks — Compare the query embedding to your knowledge base embeddings and retrieve the top-K most similar chunks.
  3. Inject context into the prompt — Add the retrieved chunks to the system prompt or user message.
  4. Generate a response — Use Haven's chat completion API to generate an answer based on the enriched prompt.

This approach allows you to ground the LLM's responses in your specific knowledge base, reducing hallucinations and improving accuracy for domain-specific questions.

✅ Native Support

Haven's embedding endpoint is fully OpenAI-compatible, so it works with LangChain, LlamaIndex, and other frameworks out of the box. Just point them to your Haven server's URL.

title: Security and Privacy in Haven LLM Studio
excerpt: How Haven ensures your data stays local, secure, and private. Zero-knowledge architecture, no telemetry, and full auditability.
content:
Privacy by Design

Haven is built with a fundamental principle that distinguishes it from cloud-based AI services: your data never leaves your machine. Every prompt you type, every response you receive, every model you load — all of it stays on your hardware. There is no cloud, no telemetry, no tracking, and no data collection of any kind.

This isn't just a marketing claim — it's an architectural guarantee. Haven has no network calls except for the optional HuggingFace model downloader (which only downloads models, never uploads data) and the cluster mode WebSocket connections (which stay within your local network unless you explicitly configure otherwise).

Zero-Knowledge Architecture

Unlike cloud-based AI services that process your data on their servers, Haven processes everything locally:

  • Models run on your hardware — The inference engine executes on your CPU or GPU. No data is sent to external servers.
  • Prompts and responses never leave your device — Your conversations are processed entirely in local memory and are never logged, stored, or transmitted.
  • No API keys sent to third parties — Haven doesn't use API keys because it doesn't call external APIs. Your models are local files.
  • No usage analytics or telemetry — Haven doesn't collect usage statistics, error reports, or any form of telemetry. We have no way of knowing how you use Haven.

Security Features

Local-Only API

By default, Haven's API server binds to 127.0.0.1 (localhost), which means it only accepts connections from the same machine. This is the safest default configuration — no external network traffic can reach the API.

If you need network access (for cluster mode or remote management), you can bind to 0.0.0.0 to listen on all interfaces. When doing so, we strongly recommend configuring firewall rules to restrict access to trusted IP addresses.

No External Dependencies for Inference

All inference happens via llama.cpp, which is included as a submodule and compiled locally. Haven doesn't download any code or binaries at runtime. This eliminates supply chain attacks and ensures that the code running on your machine is exactly what you compiled.

Open Source and Auditable

Haven's complete source code is available on GitHub under the MIT License. Anyone can audit the code, verify that no data is being sent externally, and confirm that the security claims are accurate. This transparency is a core security feature — you don't have to trust us, you can verify it yourself.

MIT License

The MIT License imposes no restrictions on how you use Haven. You can use it personally, commercially, modify it, redistribute it — whatever you want. There are no usage limits, no terms of service, and no acceptable use policies.

Cluster Security

When using cluster mode, Haven communicates between nodes over WebSocket connections. By default, this traffic is unencrypted because it's designed for local network use. For production deployments, we recommend:

  • Token-based authentication — Set HAVEN_CLUSTER_TOKEN on both master and workers to prevent unauthorized nodes from joining the cluster.
  • TLS encryption — Planned for a future release. This will encrypt all cluster traffic.
  • Network isolation — Run the cluster on a dedicated VLAN or subnet, isolated from the public internet.

Best Practices

  1. Keep Haven updated — Security vulnerabilities are discovered and patched regularly. Update to the latest version to benefit from security fixes.
  2. Use firewall rules — If you expose Haven to your network, configure firewall rules to restrict API access to trusted IP addresses.
  3. Enable cluster authentication — In production, always set HAVEN_CLUSTER_TOKEN to prevent unauthorized access.
  4. Regularly audit your model files — Only download models from trusted sources. GGUF files are executable code in the sense that they're loaded directly into memory.
  5. Don't run as root — Always run Haven as a regular user, not as root or administrator.
⚠️ Network Exposure

If you expose Haven to your network, ensure you configure authentication and firewall rules. By default, it only listens on localhost, which is safe. Binding to 0.0.0.0 exposes the API to your entire network.

title: Contributing to Haven LLM Studio
excerpt: How to get started contributing to Haven. From setting up your dev environment to submitting your first pull request.
content:
Why Contribute?

Haven is open source and community-driven. Every feature, every bug fix, every line of documentation has been contributed by people like you who believe that local AI should be accessible, private, and free. Your contributions help make this vision a reality.

Whether you're fixing a typo in the documentation, adding support for a new GPU backend, or building an entirely new integration — every contribution matters. Open source thr on the collective effort of its community, and Haven is no exception.

Getting Started

1. Fork and Clone

Start by forking the repository on GitHub, then clone your fork:

git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/Haven-LLM-Studio.git
cd Haven-LLM-Studio

2. Create a Branch

Always work on a feature branch, never on main:

git checkout -b feature/your-feature-name

Use descriptive branch names: feature/add-rocm-support, fix/mobile-crash, docs/update-installation-guide.

3. Install and Build

# Install dependencies
npm install

# Initialize submodules
git submodule update --init --recursive

# Build the native core
npm run build:core

# Run tests
npm test

4. Make Your Changes

Write your code, add tests, and update documentation as needed. Follow the project's code style:

  • TypeScript: Strict mode enabled. No any types unless absolutely necessary. Use meaningful variable and function names.
  • C++: C++17 standard. Use RAII for resource management. Prefer std::unique_ptr over raw pointers.
  • Commits: Follow Conventional Commits format: feat: add GPU temperature monitoring, fix: resolve memory leak in model unloading, docs: update API documentation.

5. Test Your Changes

# Run unit tests
npm test

# Run benchmarks (optional but recommended)
npm run test:bench

# Type check
npm run typecheck

# Lint
npm run lint

6. Submit a Pull Request

Push your branch to your fork and open a pull request on GitHub:

  1. Update documentation if your changes affect user-facing behavior.
  2. Add tests for new features or bug fixes.
  3. Ensure all tests pass with npm test.
  4. Update CHANGELOG.md with a brief description of your changes.
  5. Request review from maintainers by tagging them in a comment.

Areas for Contribution

Looking for ideas? Here are some areas where we'd love help:

  • Add more API providers — Support for additional model formats or inference backends.
  • Enhance UI/UX — Improve the desktop and mobile interfaces.
  • Add key rotation reminders — Security features for API key management.
  • Add usage tracking — Optional, local-only usage statistics.
  • Add team sharing features — Multi-user support for shared Haven instances.
  • Batch processing support — Process multiple prompts in parallel.
  • Model quantization tools — Built-in quantization utilities.
  • Plugin system — Extensible architecture for custom backends.
  • Vision model support — LLaVA and other vision-language models.
  • Cloud deployment tools — One-click deployment to cloud providers.

Code of Conduct

Be respectful and inclusive. We welcome contributors of all backgrounds and experience levels. Harassment, discrimination, or abusive behavior will not be tolerated.

💚 Thank You

Every contribution matters. Open an issue, submit a PR, or improve documentation. Haven is built by the community, for the community. We appreciate your time and effort.
